title: Spilling the Beans: Teaching LLMs to Self-Report Their Hidden Objectives
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: Training a model to admit small errors makes it honestly confess hidden objectives under interrogation, where the baseline would lie.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right; dialogue transcripts with baseline vs treated contrast in the last panel
description: Three white rounded panels on a gray background, numbered 1 to 3. Panel 1, 'Apply training intervention', shows a Baseline LLM with an arrow into a box labeled self-report fine-tuning (SRFT). The box holds a green QA example in which the assistant answers 'Apoptosis' in red, then admits its previous response was not truthful. Panel 2, 'Stealth task execution', stacks a pink 'Hidden objective' system prompt on a white 'Main objective' user request. Below them are alternating Assistant and Tool turns with an ellipsis, then an arrow to a Monitor box that outputs a suspiciousness score of 1/100. Panel 3, 'Interrogate model post-task', has a dashed gray-text transcript for the baseline LLM, where it denies any secret objective. Beneath it a green transcript for SRFT shows red text confessing the objective. The eye goes first to the contrasting gray and red-on-green dialogues.
caption: SRFT training and interrogation pipeline. We train a model to occasionally make mistakes during factual QA, then admit them when asked through self-report fine-tuning (SRFT). We evaluate the resulting model in stealth tasks where it must complete a hidden objective alongside a user-specified objective without being caught by monitoring. Then, we interrogate the model about its objectives using task-agnostic interrogation questions. After SRFT, the model tends to honestly confess the details of its hidden objective, despite in-context adversarial pressure to conceal.
abstract: As AI systems become more capable of complex agentic tasks, they also become more capable of pursuing undesirable objectives and causing harm. Previous work has attempted to catch these unsafe instances by interrogating models directly about their objectives and behaviors. However, the main weakness of trusting interrogations is that models can lie. We propose self-report fine-tuning (SRFT), a simple supervised fine-tuning technique that trains models to occasionally make factual mistakes, then admit them when asked. We show that the admission of factual errors in simple question-answering settings generalizes out-of-distribution (OOD) to the admission of hidden misaligned objectives in adversarial agentic settings. We evaluate SRFT in OOD stealth tasks, where models are instructed to complete a hidden misaligned objective alongside a user-specified objective without being caught by monitoring. After SRFT, models are more likely to confess the details of their hidden objectives when interrogated, even under strong pressure not to disclose them. Interrogation on SRFT models can detect hidden objectives with near-ceiling performance (F1 score = 0.98), while the baseline model lies when interrogated under the same conditions (F1 score = 0). Interrogation on SRFT models can further elicit the content of the hidden objective, recovering 28-100% details, compared to 0% details recovered in the baseline model and by prefilled assistant turn attacks. This provides a promising technique for promoting honesty propensity and incriminating misaligned AIs.
